body.text: Jensen Huang will not return to Nvidia as its chief executive, and for good reason.
The former Nvidia executive made an 11th-hour plea to Nvidia's board on social media earlier today.

"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he wrote.
There's no question Huang is a once-in-a-generation technology company executive.
He built Nvidia into a multi-trillion-dollar company and it became the symbol of the global artificial intelligence revolution.
But there's a pervading view his presence adds what investors call "risk" to Nvidia's valuation.
And this risk comes at a time when there is already too much of it attached to the artificial intelligence and tech industry more broadly.
Alleged spy affair too much for investors
In recent weeks speculation had swirled that Huang had been involved in an extra-marital affair.
It later emerged that the woman involved, Alice Huang, was allegedly a Chinese spy.
Soon after, reports of two other extra-marital affairs emerged, both with Nvidia staff members.
Huang will front Congress about his indiscretions tonight, Australian time.
Both the FBI and the US Justice Department are looking into how his relationship with Alice Huang could present national security concerns.
The US currently has export controls on Nvidia's powerful computer chips.
Jensen Huang was key in developing these chips (originally designed for computer games) for artificial intelligence applications.
The US is especially sensitive about China getting any information related to these chips.
Huang's liaisons with Alice Huang create a large question mark around whether any information has been leaked to China.
Any suggestion that Nvidia's technological edge might be compromised would, to say the least, be unhelpful for the tech-giant's investors.
Future revenue growth key to Huang departure
Nvidia's stock price has crashed over the space of a month, down 33 per cent from its October peak.
The stock is effectively in a bear market.
The Blue wave that enveloped the US midterm elections acted as a major circuit-breaker for the stock's valuation.
Key US states, including Texas, indicated they were not going lie down and give data centres free reign over their landscape.
Data centres are a key revenue generator for Nvidia.
So-called hyperscalers use Nvidia chips to power their data centres.
Huang's affairs added to a sense of investor insecurity about the firm's ability to lead the market on computer chips.
Groundswell of support for Huang
But Huang has enormous support and a desire to return to the helm of the company.
Despite the board's decision to oust him, the groundswell of support had many wondering whether the board would reconsider.
Chair Harvey Jones's comment on the matter this morning though left no doubt about a possible Huang return.

In a third-quarter earnings call, Mr Jones said he would not take questions about the circumstances of Mr Huang's resignation and the ongoing investigation, but backed Huang's interim replacement, Colette Kress.
"We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity and ability to deliver as interim CEO," he said, according to NBC.
And Kress, who is also finance chief, defended her team's work since Huang's departure.
"Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week," she said. "We've got this."
Analysts say Nvidia's executives are drawing a firm line in the sand to ring fence the fallout of the affairs in terms of the companies valuation.
"NVIDIA's first call since Jensen Huang stepped down was steady and business-like, marking a big shift in tone compared to Jensen's usual approach," Spaceship VP of investments Jason Sedawie said.
More to Nvidia than Huang
The bottom line is that Huang's talents are almost irrelevant to the board now.
Companies are more than just one individual, and the board has clearly placed a lot of weight on the market's perceptions of its governance practices.
All the talent in the world is useless if an organisation isn't run according to established practices.
"The reason hasn't changed: Huang is still tied to too much uncertainty and risk, which is the same reason the board pushed him out in the first place," Floodlines Research's Anna Wu said.
"It's also a good test of whether the market only believes in the rockstar, or in the numbers too," Anna Wu observed.
It seems the market has accepted that Nvidia can power on without Huang.
As Marcus Today senior analyst Henry Jennings put it: "He's not the Messiah, just a very naughty boy."
For the uninitiated, that's a reference to the famed Monty Python movie Life of Brian.
"[The] board's credibility is at stake and Jensen has become a meme, [which is] not a great look," Mr Jennings said.
"[Welcoming Huang back as Nvidia CEO] would send a message which is not conducive to good governance."
"They were a little premature in sacking him and maybe should have waited until investigation was over, but that ship has sailed,"
Jennings said.
For now, Nvidia has delivered on the numbers side, with revenue up 20 per cent for the third quarter to $US115 billion ($170 billion).

The $US3.75 trillion question is whether the tech giant, under new leadership, can better that, especially as the fallout from Huang's extramarital affairs continue to play out before the American public.
